To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the changes observed in postural control are due to changes in the plantar flexor muscles, and that they are small and not clinically relevant.

(a) the most important stabilometric parameters for describing age-related changes in quiet standing are those that describe the plantar flexion muscle torque, and (b) the most important parameters for describing the plantar flexor muscle torque are those that describe its frequency and amplitude.

(i) the use of a modern approach of stabilometry, based on a diffusion-like process, allows the identification of changes of postural control in aged subjects that are not detectable by classical analysis; (ii) the use of the proposed framework of posturology allows the interpretation of the changes of the postural control in terms of changes of the plantar flexion muscle torque.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of postural control of young, middle-aged, and aged subjects, with a special focus on the identification and interpretation of age-related changes.
the identification of the most suitable stabilometric parameters to assess postural control and to interpret the results of posturography in clinical practice.
the interpretation of the results of classical and recent stabilometric descriptors, which can be considered as a useful tool for the assessment of postural control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aging does not result in any major change of the control of postural stability.
aging is associated with a small increase of plantar flexion muscle activity, but not with a decrease of postural stability.
age-related changes in quiet standing postural control are subtle and do not result in a significant decrease in postural stability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the aging process does not affect significantly the postural control, but rather reflects the lower stiffness of the plantar flexor tendon and a higher amplitude and frequency of plantar flexion torques to maintain balance.
aging itself does not result into a major change of postural stability.

aging does not result in a major change of postural control, but reflects a minor increase of torque adjustments in the sagittal plane to compensate for the decrease of stiffness in calf muscle tendon.
The main takeaway from our work is that
classical stabilometric parameters are not able to identify age-related changes in the control of quiet standing.

the classical approach to postural control analysis may not be sufficient to identify age-related changes, and the use of more recent analysis techniques, like the one presented here, may be required.

the interpretation of stabilometric parameters should be based on the framework of postural stabilization and that the use of classical descriptors should be limited to the estimation of postural control strategies.
